name: Spanish
variant: Latin American Spanish, as spoken in Mexico and the US Southwest

units.title: Hello and goodbye
units.intro: Start with the words you use every day: hello, goodbye, please and thank you. Spanish speakers greet each other a lot, so these words open doors. Say them out loud each time you hear them.

items.note: The h is silent: say OH-lah.
Used until about noon.
Used from noon until it gets dark.
Used to say hello after dark and also good night at bedtime.
Friendly form, for family, friends and kids.
Polite form, for adults you don't know well, teachers and older people.
Tú (with an accent) means you. Tu (no accent) means your.
For small things, like bumping into someone.
Said when you walk past someone or leave the table.
To a group. To one boy or man: bienvenido. To one girl or woman: bienvenida.

tips: Spanish questions start with an upside-down question mark (¿) and exclamations with an upside-down exclamation mark (¡).
Use tú with family and friends, and usted to be polite with adults you don't know well.
Many people greet with a handshake, a hug, or a kiss on the cheek among family and friends.

units.title: Names and introductions
units.intro: Learn to say who you are, where you're from, and to meet new people. You'll also learn a few lifesaver phrases for when you don't understand. Nobody expects a beginner to be perfect, and people love it when you try.

items.note: The double L sounds like the y in yes.
A girl or woman says encantada.
Él with an accent means he. El without one means the.

items.lit: I introduce my mom to you.

items.note: Polite form, good with any adult.

items.en: How do you say it in Spanish?

tips: Me llamo and mi nombre es both mean my name is. Me llamo is the most common.
Names of languages are not capitalized in Spanish: español, inglés.

units.title: Numbers 0 to 20
units.intro: Count from zero to twenty. Numbers come up everywhere: ages, prices, phone numbers and the time. Try counting things you see out the car window.

items.note: Before a boy word it shortens to un: un perro, one dog. Before a girl word it is una: una casa.
Say OHN-seh, not like the English word once.

tips: From 16 to 19 the numbers are ten and six, ten and seven, and so on, joined into one word: dieciséis, diecisiete.
In Mexico, people often say a phone number in pairs: 52 18 is cincuenta y dos, dieciocho.

units.title: Colors
units.intro: Name the colors around you. In Spanish the color usually comes after the thing: the car red, not the red car. Many colors also change their ending to match the word they describe.

items.note: Many people also say naranja.
Also rosado.
In Mexico brown is café, like the color of coffee. Other places say marrón.
Blanco becomes blanca to match casa, a girl word.

items.es: Mi color favorito es el verde.

tips: Colors ending in o change to a for girl words: un gato negro, una gata negra.
Add s for more than one: los carros rojos. Colors ending in a consonant add es: azules, grises.

units.title: Family
units.intro: Talk about the people you love. Every Spanish noun is either a boy word (el) or a girl word (la), and family words show it clearly: el abuelo is grandpa, la abuela is grandma.

items.note: Los hermanos can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together.
A girl cousin is la prima.
It can mean two brothers, or a brother and a sister.
Te quiero is the everyday way to say I love you to family and friends.

tips: A group with at least one boy uses the boy word: los tíos can mean uncles, or aunts and uncles.
Mamá and papá have an accent on the last a: ma-MÁ, pa-PÁ.

units.title: Feelings
units.intro: Say how you feel. Spanish uses estoy (I am) for feelings that come and go, and tengo (I have) for hunger, thirst, cold and fear. Many feeling words end in o for boys and a for girls.

items.note: Feliz is the same for boys and girls.
A girl or woman says contenta.
A girl or woman says cansada.
A girl or woman says enojada.
A girl or woman says aburrida.
A girl or woman says nerviosa.
A girl or woman says emocionada.
A girl or woman says lista.
Say tengo calor when you feel hot. Estoy caliente means something different.

tips: Estoy comes from estar, the verb for how you are right now. Soy comes from ser, the verb for who you are.
Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, sleepiness and fear use tengo: you have them, you aren't them.

units.title: Numbers to 100 and age
units.intro: Count up to one hundred and tell your age. From 31 on, numbers join with y (and): treinta y uno is thirty-one. To give your age you say how many years you have.

items.note: Numbers 21 to 29 are one word.
Exactly 100 is cien. From 101 on it is ciento: ciento uno.

items.lit: How many years do you have?

items.es: Mi papá tiene cuarenta y dos años.

tips: Sesenta (60) and setenta (70) sound alike. Listen for the middle: se-SEN-ta, se-TEN-ta.
Always say años (years). Without the wavy line over the n, the word means something else.

units.title: Days, months and dates
units.intro: Learn the days of the week, the months, and how to say a date. Days and months are not capitalized in Spanish. Dates go day first, then month: the fifth of May.

items.es: Mi cumpleaños es el diez de marzo.
items.lit: My birthday is the ten of March.

items.note: For the first of the month, people usually say primero (first).

tips: The week starts on Monday (lunes) on Spanish calendars.
To say on Saturday, use el: el sábado. Every Saturday is los sábados.

units.title: Time of day and telling time
units.intro: Talk about today, tomorrow and yesterday, and tell the time. For one o'clock you say es la una; for every other hour you say son las. Add y (and) for minutes after the hour.

items.note: Mañana also means morning. Tomorrow morning is mañana por la mañana.

items.lit: They are the three and a half.

items.note: Common in Mexico. Other places say son las doce menos cuarto.

items.es: Son las ocho de la mañana.
Son las nueve de la noche.

tips: Es la una because una (one) is just one hour. Son las dos because two and up are more than one.
Use de la mañana, de la tarde and de la noche instead of a.m. and p.m.

units.title: Food and drinks
units.intro: Name everyday foods and drinks and talk at the table. Many of these words are already familiar in Arizona: tortilla, frijoles, queso. Listen for the el or la in front of each one.

items.note: Agua is a girl word, but it takes el because it starts with a stressed a.
In Mexico the big midday meal is often called la comida.

items.en: Can you pass me the salt?

items.note: Rico about food means tasty, not rich.
People say it to others who are eating, even strangers at a restaurant.

tips: Meals: el desayuno (breakfast), el almuerzo or la comida (lunch), la cena (dinner).
To ask for food politely, add por favor, and say gracias when it arrives.

units.title: At home
units.intro: Name the rooms and things in your house and practice the things families say every day. Many of these are short commands, the way a parent talks to a kid.

items.note: In Mexico a bedroom is also called la recámara.
El sillón is a big armchair, though some people use it for a couch too.
Short for la televisión.
Also ven aquí.
Common in Mexico. Also enciende la luz.

tips: En casa means at home, without la: Estoy en casa.
Commands to one person you know well, like ven, cierra and apaga, are the tú form.

units.title: School and the classroom
units.intro: Words and phrases for school: the things in your backpack and what teachers and students say in class. Great for kids to practice on the way to school.

items.note: A man teacher is el maestro.
Also el salón de clases.
More than one: los lápices.
Pen in Mexico. Other places say el bolígrafo.

items.en: May I go to the bathroom?

items.note: Said to the whole class.
Sé with an accent means I know.

tips: Kids in Mexico often call their teacher maestra or maestro, or just profe.
Abran (open, to a group) uses the ustedes form, which is how you talk to more than one person.

units.title: In the car and directions
units.intro: Phrases for road trips and getting around: left, right, straight, near and far. Practice them right where you are, in the car. Watch out for derecha (right) and derecho (straight): one letter makes the difference.

items.note: Also el coche or el auto.
Also dobla a la izquierda.
Derecho means straight. Derecha means right.
Here para means stop, from parar.

tips: Use está for where something is: Está cerca, it's close.
Vamos means both we're going and let's go.

units.title: Shopping and money
units.intro: Ask prices, pay and shop for clothes. Most of these are polite phrases you would use with a store clerk, so they use usted.

items.note: Often used to ask for the total.
In Mexico you'll also hear nada más estoy viendo.
Polite, used when handing something over.

tips: Cuesta is for one thing, cuestan for more than one: ¿Cuánto cuestan los zapatos?
In Mexico, money is often called lana in casual talk. It's slang, so use dinero when in doubt.

units.title: Weather and seasons
units.intro: Talk about the weather, a favorite topic in Arizona. Spanish uses hace (it makes) for most weather: hace calor, it's hot. For things happening right now, like rain, it uses está.
tips: Hace calor is about the weather; tengo calor is about how you feel.
Seasons use el or la: en el verano, in the summer.

units.title: The body and the doctor
units.intro: Name parts of the body and say what hurts. Spanish says it hurts me: me duele la cabeza, my head hurts. If more than one thing hurts, it becomes me duelen.

items.note: La mano is a girl word even though it ends in o.
A girl or woman says enferma.
Also el médico.
Said after a sneeze. It also means cheers when people raise a glass.

tips: Spanish says la cabeza (the head), not mi cabeza (my head), when it's clear whose head it is.
Me duele for one thing, me duelen for more than one.

units.title: Animals and the desert
units.intro: Pets and the creatures of the Sonoran Desert right outside your door. Many Arizona place names and animal names come from Spanish, like the correcaminos (roadrunner), which literally means road runner.

items.note: A live fish. Fish as food is el pescado.
In Sonora and Arizona Spanish the javelina is usually called jabalí. Its other name is pecarí.
Many people in Mexico also say halcón (falcon) or aguililla.
The giant cactus of the Sonoran Desert.
Used in Arizona. In Mexico people usually say la temporada de lluvias, the rainy season.

tips: Sahuarita's name is said to come from sahuarito, a little saguaro, the cactus you see all around town.
El correcaminos stays the same for more than one: los correcaminos.

units.title: At a restaurant
units.intro: Order food, ask questions about the menu and pay the check. Quisiera (I would like) is a very polite way to order. In Mexico, pica means spicy, and it's a good word to know.

items.es: Una mesa para cuatro, por favor.

items.note: A waitress is la mesera.

items.en: What do you want to drink?
items.note: Tomar here means to drink.

items.es: Un vaso de agua, por favor.

items.note: A girl or woman says llena.

tips: In many restaurants in Mexico the server won't bring the check until you ask for it. It's polite, not slow.
Quisiera is softer than quiero, like I'd like versus I want.

units.title: Everyday verbs
units.intro: Put the most useful verbs to work: ser and estar (to be), tener (to have), ir (to go), querer (to want) and poder (can). Each one changes its ending to show who is doing it: voy is I go, vamos is we go.

items.note: About a boy or man: simpático.

items.es: Mi mamá está en el trabajo.

items.note: Tener que plus a verb means to have to.
Al is a plus el: a el trabajo becomes al trabajo.

tips: Ser is for what someone or something is (a student, from Arizona, nice). Estar is for where it is and how it is right now (in the car, tired).
Spanish often leaves out I, you and we, because the verb ending already says who: tengo means I have.

units.title: Asking questions
units.intro: The question words: qué (what), dónde (where), cuándo (when), quién (who), por qué (why), cuánto (how much), cuál (which) and cómo (how). Question words always have an accent mark. Your voice goes up at the end of a yes-or-no question.

items.en: What do you want to do?

items.note: Why is por qué, two words. Because is porque, one word.

items.en: How much water do you want?
How many brothers and sisters do you have?

items.note: To a group. To one boy: ¿Listo? To one girl: ¿Lista?

tips: Cuánto changes to match: cuánto tiempo, cuánta agua, cuántos años, cuántas horas.
Qué, dónde and cuándo have accents in questions, and no accent when they aren't asking: que, donde, cuando.

units.title: Likes and dislikes
units.intro: Say what you like with gustar. It works backward from English: me gusta el chocolate means chocolate pleases me. Use gusta for one thing or an action, and gustan for more than one thing.

items.note: Gustan, because dogs are more than one.
Fútbol is soccer. American football is el fútbol americano.

items.en: Yes, I like it a lot.
items.note: Sí with an accent means yes. Si without one means if.

items.en: He likes to draw. / She likes to draw.

items.es: A mi hermana le gusta bailar.

items.en: We like going to the park.
What do you like to do?

items.note: To agree when someone likes something.
To agree when someone doesn't like something.

items.en: I don't like it at all.
Which one do you like better?

tips: Me gusta (I like), te gusta (you like), le gusta (he or she likes), nos gusta (we like), les gusta (they like).
Use the with things you like in general: me gusta el chocolate, not me gusta chocolate.

units.title: Making plans
units.intro: Talk about what's going to happen with ir a plus a verb: voy a comer, I'm going to eat. It's the easiest way to talk about the future, and you already know the pieces.

items.note: It can also mean we're going to play.

items.en: I'm going to do my homework.

items.es: Voy a llamar a mi abuela.
items.en: I'm going to call my grandma.
What are you going to do today?

items.es: Este fin de semana vamos a visitar a los abuelos.
items.en: This weekend we're going to visit Grandma and Grandpa.
We're going to watch a movie.

items.es: Vamos a comer pizza esta noche.
items.en: We're going to eat pizza tonight.
What are we having for dinner?
My dad is going to cook.

items.es: Vamos a salir en cinco minutos.

items.en: Afterward we're going to the store.

items.es: Primero la tarea, luego a jugar.

tips: Voy a, vas a, va a, vamos a, van a, then the verb as it is in the dictionary: comer, jugar, dormir.
Put a before a person you visit or call: visitar a los abuelos, llamar a mi abuela.

units.title: What happened
units.intro: Tell what you did, using the past tense in short, ready-made phrases. Learn them whole for now: fui (I went), comí (I ate), jugué (I played). They're perfect for answering how was your day.

items.lit: How did it go for you at school?

items.en: Yesterday I went to the park.
I had a lot of fun.
It rained a lot last night.

tips: Many past forms for I end in an accented é or í: hablé, terminé, comí, aprendí. The accent changes the meaning, so stress the end.
Fui means both I went and I was. The rest of the sentence makes it clear.

units.title: Conversation in the car
units.intro: A review unit made of a real family car ride, from buckling up to arriving at Grandma's. Try answering each line yourself before you hear the Spanish.

items.en: Does everyone have their seat belt on?

items.es: Vamos a casa de la abuela.

items.en: Can you turn up the volume?

items.es: Hace mucho calor en el carro.
items.en: It's really hot in the car.
Can you turn on the AC?
items.note: El aire here means the air conditioning.
Mucha, because hambre is a girl word.

items.es: ¿Qué fue lo mejor de tu día?
items.en: What was the best part of your day?

tips: Spanish often uses the present for the near future: Llegamos en diez minutos, we'll be there in ten minutes.
Ya means already or now. ¿Ya llegamos? asks are we there yet; ¡Ya llegamos! says we're here.
